chapters.title: Chapter 6: Evaluating a Market Making Business

lessons.title: Spread Capture Rate and Fill Ratio: The Two Numbers That Actually Matter

body.text: A single day's P&L cannot tell you whether a market making business is actually working. Two quieter numbers, how much of the quoted spread you actually keep, and how often your quote gets hit at all, tell you far more.

children.text: Why P&L Alone Doesn't Tell You If the Business Is Working

Chapter 3's case study showed a single day's P&L made up of steady spread income from calm periods, netted against the cost of managing a risky inventory buildup during a volatile one. Look only at the final number and a good day of disciplined risk management can look identical to a bad day the desk simply got lucky on. Evaluating whether the core quoting business itself is sound, separate from how well or badly a specific risk episode was handled, needs metrics that isolate the quoting mechanism from the noise of individual risk events.
Spread Capture Rate: How Much of the Quoted Spread You Actually Keep

markDefs.definition: The average realised profit per completed round-trip trade, divided by the average quoted spread at the time those trades happened. It measures how much of the theoretical spread a market maker actually converts into real profit, rather than losing to adverse price movement between opening and closing a position.

children.text: The quoted spread from Chapter 1 is a theoretical number: it is what a market maker would earn on a trade that opened and closed instantly with no price movement in between. Real round trips rarely work that way, since a position bought at the bid usually has to be held, even briefly, before it can be sold at the ask, and the price can drift during that gap.
measures how much of that theoretical spread actually survives into realised profit once every completed round trip is accounted for.

body.latex: \text{Spread Capture Rate} = \frac{\text{Average Realised Profit per Round Trip}}{\text{Average Quoted Spread}}
body.caption: A spread capture rate of 100% means every round trip earned exactly the quoted spread; anything lower reflects price movement eating into that theoretical edge between opening and closing a position.

body.label: Worked Example
body.context: Average quoted spread of ₹0.10, average realised profit per round trip of ₹0.07: 0.07 ÷ 0.10 = 70%. Three-tenths of the theoretical spread was lost to price movement and other frictions between opening and closing positions.

children.text: Fill Ratio: How Often Your Quote Actually Gets Hit

markDefs.definition: The proportion of a market maker's quotes that actually result in a trade, out of the total number of quotes posted over a given period. A very low fill ratio is normal for a continuously requoting market maker, since most cancel-and-replace messages never get hit at all.

children.text: Recall from Chapter 5 that a market maker's apparently stable quote is really a rapid stream of cancel-and-replace messages. Most of those messages never actually trade; they are simply superseded by the next update before anyone hits them.

measures what fraction do. A fill ratio of even a few percent can be entirely normal for an active quoting strategy, since the number itself matters less on its own than what it implies when read alongside spread capture rate.

body.label: Worked Example
body.context: 10,000 quotes posted across a session, 250 of them resulted in an actual trade: 250 ÷ 10,000 = 2.5%. The other 97.5% were cancelled or replaced before anyone traded against them, which is ordinary behaviour for a fast-requoting market maker, not evidence of a problem on its own.

body.caption: Reading spread capture rate and fill ratio together

cells: A healthy core business: competitively priced quotes that get hit often and mostly convert into real profit
Good margin per trade, but quotes may be too wide or too passive, losing queue priority and volume to competitors
A warning sign: getting hit constantly but not converting spread into profit, consistent with heavy adverse selection from Chapter 4
Weak on both fronts, suggesting the underlying pricing model itself may be mismatched to this instrument

body.text: The low-capture, high-fill quadrant is the one worth watching most closely. A market maker getting hit constantly while its spread capture rate deteriorates is describing, in two operational numbers, exactly the situation Chapter 4 built PIN and VPIN to detect: order flow that is more informed than the quote was priced for.

body.title: Computing a Weaker Spread Capture Rate
body.prompt: A different desk has an average quoted spread of ₹0.08 and an average realised profit per round trip of only ₹0.02. What is its spread capture rate, as a percentage?
body.explanation: 0.02 ÷ 0.08 = 0.25, or 25%. Three-quarters of this desk's theoretical spread is being lost between opening and closing positions, a far weaker outcome than the 70% worked example earlier in this lesson, and worth investigating alongside this desk's fill ratio before concluding whether the problem is adverse selection, poor inventory management, or something else.

body.text: A market maker chasing a higher fill ratio by quoting tighter and tighter, without watching what happens to spread capture rate at the same time, can end up winning far more queue priority on trades that are individually worth less, or even net negative, exactly the kind of pattern that also tends to show up as a concerning order-to-trade ratio under Chapter 5's regulatory framework.

body.title: Diagnosing a Desk From Its Numbers
body.question: A desk reports a fill ratio that has risen sharply over the past month while its spread capture rate has fallen at the same time. What does this combination most likely indicate?
options: The desk has become more profitable, since it is trading more often
The desk's quotes have become more competitive and are increasingly being hit by order flow that is more informed than the pricing model accounts for
The desk's risk-processing costs have increased for unrelated reasons
This combination is impossible; fill ratio and spread capture rate always move together
body.explanation: A rising fill ratio paired with a falling spread capture rate is the low-capture, high-fill quadrant from this lesson's table: the desk is being hit more often, but converting less of the theoretical spread into real profit on each hit, which is consistent with facing more informed, harder-to-price-correctly order flow than before, not simply becoming more active.

points: P&L alone conflates the quality of a market maker's core quoting business with the outcome of specific risk episodes, so it is a poor standalone metric for evaluating the business itself
Spread capture rate compares realised round-trip profit to the theoretical quoted spread, showing how much of that theoretical edge survives real price movement
Fill ratio measures how often a quote actually gets hit relative to how often it is posted, and a low number on its own is normal for a fast-requoting market maker
Reading the two together, using the quadrant framework, reveals patterns neither metric shows alone, especially a falling spread capture rate paired with a rising fill ratio
That specific combination is an operational early-warning sign of the same adverse selection risk Chapter 4 built PIN and VPIN to detect
The next lesson turns to a third metric, inventory turnover and holding time, which measures the risk side of the business rather than its profitability
